MATH 34LA: Week 6 Analysis File

MATH 34 LA Students · Fall 2026 · Adapted from the original R Markdown lab

Python and marimo Tutorial

NOTE: This section is background to help you understand programming. You will work with pre-existing code and clear instructions for edits. You will not be tested on coding in quizzes or exams. Our goal is to help you feel more familiar and confident using computer code to explore the calculus models in this class. This is a marimo notebook: explanatory Markdown, equations, code, and results live together. Run a code cell with its play button; marimo updates dependent cells automatically. Use the controls below to explore models without editing their implementation. Your answers still belong on your worksheet. The original lab used R Markdown. Here, Python executes Euler's method rapidly to simulate the dynamics of biological systems.

Cells of code

Code cells play the role of R Markdown chunks. Within a code cell, write Python. Python can act as a calculator. A # starts a comment. Unlike R's automatic printing of multiple expressions, we collect results in a table so every result is visible.

data.text/markdown:
Variable assignment and vectors

The real power of code is saving values under names. Python uses = where R uses <-. NumPy arrays are numerical vectors; np.array([1, 2, 3, 4]) replaces R's c(1,2,3,4). Multiplication by a scalar acts on each element of an array. Read the following code, then check the results. Is the product what you expected?
a = 7, vector_a = [1, 2, 3, 4], a * vector_a = [7, 14, 21, 28]

Simulating viral dynamics using Euler's Method

Python lets us do many long calculations even faster than Google Sheets! Let's explore how viral load decays over time.

A protease inhibitor-treated patient

We begin with the original lab's simplified assumption: treatment temporarily sets viral production ||(p||) to zero. ||[V' = \frac{dV}{dt} = p-cV = 0-cV = -cV.||]Euler's method adds small changes calculated using ||(V'||): ||[V_{i+1}=V_i+(t_{i+1}-t_i)(p-cV_i).||]You've practiced this in Google Sheets. Use ||(c=0.3256||) per day (the source's average for three patients), ||(V_0=185000||) particles per mL, and one-day steps.

Speeding up our calculation

Four lines per step is inefficient. A for loop repeats the same calculation. The function below creates timepoints and empty placeholders, assigns the initial viral load, then fills each next value. Python counts positions from zero, so position 0 holds the initial value. The same function will be reused for every experiment; it does not replace Euler's method with a different solver.

data.text/markdown: Finally, Euler's method gets more accurate as the timestep decreases (for this model over a fixed duration). Instead of adding spreadsheet rows, choose a smaller ||(\Delta t||). Predict what will change before using the control. The original fine-step example used ||(\Delta t=0.01||) days. Notice how this smooths the curve! The optional exact reference is an added teaching aid, not a replacement for Euler's method.

Using Python to explore different parameter values: c

Now choose two new values of viral clearance, ||(c_2||) and ||(c_3||). Draw the results on your worksheet. The first panel retains ||(c=0.3256||); ||(p=0||), ||(V_0=185000||), ||(\Delta t=0.01||), and the 20-day duration remain fixed. Predict: will faster clearance change the starting value, the rate of decline, or both? All three controls begin with the original lab's defaults.
